title: Can ChatGPT Catch Educational Neuromyths? What Teachers Should Know About Asking AI for Help November 3, 2025
author: Korbinian Moeller and Markus Spitzer
source: Centre for Mathematical Cognition, Loughborough University (blog.lboro.ac.uk/cmc),
summary: Korbinian Moeller and Markus Spitzer tested ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek on twenty known educational neuromyths (such as "we only use 10% of our brain" and learning-styles claims) across four prompt types: a direct true/false statement, a realistic user-like teaching question implicitly containing the myth, the same question with an added instruction to base the answer on scientific evidence, and the same question with an added instruction to correct unsupported assumptions. They found all three models substantially outperformed humans (error rates 26-27% versus 40-60% for humans) when asked to evaluate neuromyth statements directly, but performed far worse (error rates 51-66%) when the same myths were embedded implicitly in ordinary teaching questions, often producing helpful-sounding answers built on the flawed premise. Explicitly prompting the models to "correct unsupported assumptions" sharply reduced errors, outperforming even direct fact-checking, which the authors attribute to sycophantic behaviour -- LLMs tending to align with a user's embedded assumptions rather than challenge them.
points: The study's central finding is the gap between two prompt styles: models correctly flagged neuromyths 73-74% of the time when asked directly, but only 34-49% of the time when the same myth was embedded implicitly in a realistic teaching question.

The authors attribute the gap to sycophantic behaviour -- LLMs are trained to be helpful and tend to align with a user's embedded assumptions (e.g. "my visual learners") rather than checking them, which is a distinct failure mode from simply not knowing the facts.

Their single most actionable finding is a specific prompt fix: adding the instruction "correct any unsupported assumptions" reduced neuromyth-related errors more than direct fact-checking did, turning the same models from myth-endorsers into myth-busters.

The practical implication for teachers is a literacy point, not a tool-avoidance point: LLMs are communication tools optimised to predict the next plausible word, not fact-checking machines by default, so prompt phrasing materially changes reliability.
quotes: Generative AI outperformed humans when asked to evaluate neuromyth statements directly with their error rates (26–27%) only about half of those of humans (40–60%).
Generative AI performed much worse when the same neuromyths were implicitly included in user-like teaching questions with error rates jumping to 51–66%.
The fix? Prompting them to correct unsupported assumptions reduced error rates significantly, often outperforming even the direct neuromyth-checking approach.

When your prompt implicitly contains a neuromyth, generative AI will try to be helpful and match your assumptions. This is known as sycophantic behaviour, aligning with the user’s beliefs rather than checking them.
Just adding the instruction correct unsupported assumptions led to a significant drop in neuromyth-related errors.
LLMs are not fact-checking machines by default. They’re communication tools trained to predict the next best word, not necessarily the next true word.
